experiments.title: Which perceptual loss: grid, native or none?
experiments.summary: The same X5-conditioned generator trained with LPIPS on the 256 px HR grid, with LPIPS on the native 64 px LR, without LPIPS, and with grid LPIPS plus a discriminator.
experiments.purpose: Grid metrics had rejected native LPIPS, but only the native LR output is used. Losses that act only at native size leave the content inside each 4×4 block free, which grid metrics punish even though it never reaches the LR.
setup: 744 test crops, last checkpoint, native 64 px output

tables.title: Quality on the native 64 px LR (seed 0 / seed 1)
tables.note: Lower is better for LPIPS, DISTS and FID; the best mean of the two seeds is bold. FID differs by up to ~4 points between seeds. PSNR is not used for selection.

tables.title: Realism analysis
tables.note: Mean of both seeds. Noise / detail / HF power / saturation are generated ÷ real (1 = real); a real LR round-tripped through the same measurement reaches only 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.85 / 1.00. Slopes: how much of the real per-camera spread is reproduced (1 = all). z_std: output change per unit of input noise, over the real noise level. Diversity: LPIPS between outputs for different noise.

findings: Native LPIPS is best on LPIPS and DISTS on both seeds; on FID it ties with the discriminator run (37.5 vs 37.4).
Removing LPIPS is clearly worse (FID about 47 vs 38), although its outputs vary most with the noise input.
The discriminator gives the best camera-detail slope and uses the noise input most, at a small PSNR cost.
experiments.verdict: Use native LPIPS. Grid metrics were misleading for native-only losses.

experiments.title: Reference size: 64 px vs 128 px (X5)
experiments.summary: The X5 encoder sees the centre 64 px of the 128 px native reference instead of all of it.
experiments.purpose: Hand-picked references are small; check how much is lost when the reference is 64 px (256 px of HR area).
setup: grid LPIPS 2.0, native low-pass MSE, native PSD

tables.title: Quality on the native 64 px LR (seed 0 / seed 1)
tables.note: Lower is better for LPIPS, DISTS and FID; the best mean of the two seeds is bold. FID differs by up to ~4 points between seeds. PSNR is not used for selection.

tables.title: Realism analysis
tables.note: Mean of both seeds. Noise / detail / HF power / saturation are generated ÷ real (1 = real); a real LR round-tripped through the same measurement reaches only 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.85 / 1.00. Slopes: how much of the real per-camera spread is reproduced (1 = all). z_std: output change per unit of input noise, over the real noise level. Diversity: LPIPS between outputs for different noise.

findings: Quality is within seed noise; training loss was about 5% higher with 64 px.
The 64 px reference reproduces slightly less of the per-camera detail spread.
experiments.verdict: 64 px references are usable at a small cost.

experiments.title: Degradation encoder: DEResNet vs X5
experiments.summary: The frozen DEResNet (S3Diff, 256-d) replaces X5 as the degradation encoder, at 128 px and 64 px references.
experiments.purpose: X5 sees the hand-cropped references as almost identical; DEResNet separates them more. Does the generator benefit?
setup: grid LPIPS 2.0, native low-pass MSE, native PSD

tables.title: Quality on the native 64 px LR (seed 0 / seed 1)
tables.note: Lower is better for LPIPS, DISTS and FID; the best mean of the two seeds is bold. FID differs by up to ~4 points between seeds. PSNR is not used for selection.

tables.title: Realism analysis
tables.note: Mean of both seeds. Noise / detail / HF power / saturation are generated ÷ real (1 = real); a real LR round-tripped through the same measurement reaches only 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.85 / 1.00. Slopes: how much of the real per-camera spread is reproduced (1 = all). z_std: output change per unit of input noise, over the real noise level. Diversity: LPIPS between outputs for different noise.

findings: DEResNet and X5 tie within seed noise at both reference sizes.
Neither encoder makes the generator transfer noise or JPEG; outputs follow mainly blur.
experiments.verdict: No reason to switch encoders on these metrics alone.

experiments.title: Hand-cropped references: what the encoders see
experiments.summary: Four hand-cropped 64 px LR references (two labelled low degradation, two high) applied to three hand-cropped HR crops, with fixed noise per HR.
experiments.purpose: Check whether the generator follows the user-labelled degradation, and whether the encoders can tell the references apart.

tables.title: X5 cosine similarity between the references
tables.note: X5 sees all four as almost the same.

tables.title: DEResNet cosine similarity between the references
tables.note: DEResNet separates them more, but part of the spread is image content, not degradation.

figures.caption: X5 64 px model on the hand crops (seed 0)
DEResNet 64 px model on the hand crops (seed 0)

findings: Outputs follow how blurry the reference is (lowdeg2 softest, highdeg sharpest), not the user labels.
Noise and JPEG artefacts of the references are not transferred.
A downscaled HR with no degradation scores up to 0.93 against a reference of similar content, so DEResNet similarity mixes content and degradation.
experiments.verdict: The encoders separate references mainly by blur; the generator responds to that one axis.

experiments.title: All-native DEResNet 64 px, with and without a discriminator
experiments.summary: Every loss at native resolution (LPIPS moved to the native LR) with the DEResNet 64 px reference, then a native discriminator added on top.
experiments.purpose: Repeat the native-LPIPS gain with DEResNet, and test whether a discriminator adds realism.
setup: native low-pass MSE 1.0, native LPIPS 2.0, native PSD 0.1

tables.title: Quality on the native 64 px LR (seed 0 / seed 1)
tables.note: Lower is better for LPIPS, DISTS and FID; the best mean of the two seeds is bold. FID differs by up to ~4 points between seeds. PSNR is not used for selection.

tables.title: Realism analysis
tables.note: Mean of both seeds. Noise / detail / HF power / saturation are generated ÷ real (1 = real); a real LR round-tripped through the same measurement reaches only 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.85 / 1.00. Slopes: how much of the real per-camera spread is reproduced (1 = all). z_std: output change per unit of input noise, over the real noise level. Diversity: LPIPS between outputs for different noise.

tables.title: Degradation matching (DEResNet on the hand-cropped references)
tables.note: 3 HR crops × 4 references × 2 seeds, native 64 px. The four references are 0.761 similar to each other, so outputs should spread about as much. "Own ranked closest" is chance at 25%; lowdeg2 and highdeg2 are near twins (0.98), so 100% is not reachable.

figures.caption: All-native + discriminator on the hand crops (seed 0)

findings: All-native beats grid LPIPS on both seeds: LPIPS −7%, FID about 2.5 points better.
The discriminator matches per-camera detail much better (slope about 0.97) and uses the noise input more, with FID unchanged.
Neither makes outputs follow the reference: own reference ranked closest only 25% of the time (chance).
experiments.verdict: All-native is the best on quality; adding the discriminator is the best on realism.

experiments.title: Contrastive degradation loss (soft-target InfoNCE)
experiments.summary: Each HR crop is generated with four references from the batch (same noise). For each reference, DEResNet must pick the output it produced among those four; near-identical references share the target. Tried at weights 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1, and at 0.05 and 0.1 with the discriminator.
experiments.purpose: Outputs did not follow their reference. Comparing outputs that share the same HR content means content cannot decide the answer, only degradation can.

tables.note: Lower is better for LPIPS, DISTS and FID; the best mean of the two seeds is bold. FID differs by up to ~4 points between seeds. PSNR is not used for selection.

tables.note: Mean of both seeds. Noise / detail / HF power / saturation are generated ÷ real (1 = real); a real LR round-tripped through the same measurement reaches only 0.92 / 0.94 / 0.85 / 1.00. Slopes: how much of the real per-camera spread is reproduced (1 = all). z_std: output change per unit of input noise, over the real noise level. Diversity: LPIPS between outputs for different noise.

tables.title: Degradation matching (DEResNet on the hand-cropped references)
tables.note: 3 HR crops × 4 references × 2 seeds, native 64 px. The four references are 0.761 similar to each other, so outputs should spread about as much. "Own ranked closest" is chance at 25%; lowdeg2 and highdeg2 are near twins (0.98), so 100% is not reachable.

figures.caption: Degradation loss 0.1 on the hand crops (seed 0)
Degradation loss 0.1 + discriminator on the hand crops (seed 0)

findings: The loss is the only change that makes outputs follow their reference: up to 54% own-reference ranking vs 25%, with output spread close to the references.
It costs quality at every weight; 0.02 already costs about 3 FID points with no matching gain.
The discriminator recovers part of the cost and restores noise-input use: 0.1 + disc keeps 54% matching with FID 40.5 vs 41.8 alone.
experiments.verdict: A trade-off: all-native for quality, degradation loss 0.1 + discriminator for reference-following.

experiments.title: Textured reference sweep and a stripe artefact
experiments.summary: The DRealSR reference sweep now keeps the least flat of 16 random crops per photo (--texture-candidates 16, protocol v2_textured), over 6 test photos; the old sweep often landed on blank walls.
experiments.purpose: Look at how outputs change with the reference on textured content, and find where fine stripes come from.
setup: hr2lr.reference_sweep, 6 sources, 2 cross-capture references + the matched one
findings: Faint horizontal stripes on flat regions appear in all-native too, not only with the degradation loss or the discriminator; the grid-LPIPS model was smooth.
Likely cause (not yet confirmed): with every loss at native size, nothing constrains the pattern inside each 4×4 block.
With the degradation loss, the Canon reference makes the grass much more contrasty; with the striped-fabric reference a faint woven texture appears, which looks like reference content leaking in.
experiments.verdict: Next: test the stripes with a small grid-level loss or a blurred downscale, and check content leakage with same-scene ×2/×3/×4 references.
